title: Mirik College: Portfolio | Studio 1947
description: Capacity building through training beyond the classroom. A collaboration between Studio 1947 and the Department of Geography at Mirik College.

hero.alt: The Mirik College geography students and the Studio 1947 team standing together on a hill road above the Darjeeling valley at the start of fieldwork

sections.heading: Context & The Vision
sections.label: The Mission
body: What happens when you take geography out of the textbook and drop it in the middle of the Darjeeling hills? Together with the Department of Geography at Mirik College, we designed a 60-hour intensive programme. It blended classroom learning, hands-on workshops, and fieldwork into one big cauldron.

sections.label: Core Problem
body: Instead of only hearing about livelihoods, communities, and how people relate to nature, students needed to experience them first-hand. The aim was simple: learning should not stop at notes and exams. It should move, ask questions, and sometimes feel uncomfortable in a good way. Geography is not abstract. It lives in people's homes, work, and everyday decisions.

sections.heading: How the Programme Was Built
body: The programme had three parts. Each built on the last and moved students from theory to practice. More than academic activity, practical training, and on-ground discovery, it was built around curiosity and experience.

media.alt: Mirik College geography students gathered with the project team during the intensive 60-hour programme

cards.title: Classroom-Based Component (20 Hours)
cards.body: The project began in the classroom. Students were introduced to key ideas around livelihoods, settlement patterns, regional development, and how people relate to their environment. These sessions helped them place tea gardens in a wider geographic and social context, so they could approach the field with curiosity and care.

cards.title: Interactive Workshop Component (20 Hours)
cards.body: Workshops led jointly by faculty members and the Studio 1947 team shifted the focus from learning about research to learning how to do it. Students were trained in ethical field engagement, basic data collection, and writing an overall report. We talked not only about what questions to ask, but how to ask them, and why listening matters as much as writing down the answers.

cards.title: Fieldwork Component (20 Hours)
cards.body: Fieldwork was the heart of the project. This is where classroom concepts met lived experience, and where students began to see geography as something shaped by people's daily lives.

sections.heading: Field Sites & Method
body: The survey took place in Mandir Goan (Soureni) and Phuguri, two villages a short distance from Mirik. We chose these sites to understand everyday life in tea plantation areas and to let students observe working and living conditions up close.

media.alt: Mandir Goan (Soureni), the first survey village set among the tea plantations near Mirik
Phuguri Village, the second survey site, where students recorded working and living conditions

body: Students visited households directly and ran face-to-face surveys on income sources, employment patterns, access to basic services, and household challenges. Walking from home to home, listening to personal accounts, and noticing the surroundings grounded the survey data in real experience.

sections.heading: The Team & After the Field
sections.label: The Team
body: Five students from the Department of Geography, Mirik College.
One faculty member from Mirik College, providing academic guidance throughout.
Three members from Studio 1947, supporting research design, field coordination, and analysis.
This structure let students learn within an academic framework while also seeing how professional research works, with mentors alongside them.

sections.label: Post-Fieldwork Phase
body: Fieldwork was not the end of the learning. Once the surveys were done, students visited the Studio 1947 office every week and worked closely with the team to reflect on what they had found.

These 20 hours of sessions focused on organising survey responses, analysing the data, and discussing what it revealed about livelihoods in the two villages. We guided students through turning raw information into clear, structured written reports. This phase felt much like an internship, with steady mentorship and practical exposure beyond routine coursework.

media.alt: Students working with the Studio 1947 team during the post-fieldwork analysis sessions

sections.heading: Outcomes
body: The project produced a detailed, ground-level understanding of livelihood conditions, based entirely on primary data the students collected themselves.

Beyond the research output, the process built students' confidence in doing fieldwork, engaging with communities respectfully, and connecting theory with observation. At the end, all students received certificates issued by Studio 1947.
Capacity building is a core focus of Studio 1947. This collaboration showed how academic learning gets stronger when paired with real-world engagement.

Through classroom sessions, interactive workshops, and fieldwork, students developed practical research skills alongside theory. More than a single study, the project strengthened student capacity and laid the ground for future collaborations.
